stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to progressive dyspnea over the last 2 days.  The patient's exercise tolerance has decreased dramatically and she had to sleep in a sitting position last night.  She has no history of cardiovascular disease.  The patient does not use tobacco or alcohol.  Family history is unremarkable.  Blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg and pulse is 105/min and regular.  The apical impulse is hyperdynamic.  Cardiac auscultation reveals a diminished S1 and an apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla.  Diffuse pulmonary crackles are heard bilaterally.  There is no peripheral edema.  ECG shows sinus tachycardia but is otherwise unremarkable.  Which of the following would most likely increase the ratio of forward flow volume to regurgitant flow volume in this patient?​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​

options.label: C
options.text: Decreasing venous return to the left ventricle

options.label: E
options.text: Increasing venous return to the left ventricle

explanation:
This patient's dyspnea, orthopnea, and crackles on lung auscultation are consistent with decompensated left-sided heart failure; the apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla further suggests underlying mitral regurgitation (MR).  In patients with MR, some of the blood in the left ventricle (LV) is pumped forward through the aortic valve (forward stroke volume), and some is forced backward through the incompetent mitral valve (regurgitant stroke volume).  The amount of blood flowing down each pathway is determined by the relative resistance between the two:

  • Forward flow is impeded by the pressure in the aorta (ie, systolic blood pressure).

  • Regurgitant flow is restricted by the mitral valve orifice size and the degree of left atrial compliance (ie, left atrial pressure during ventricular systole).

With chronic MR, left atrial pressure remains relatively constant over the short term, but aortic pressure can vary significantly with changes in systemic vascular resistance (SVR).  A reduction in SVR leads to reduced systemic blood pressure and an increase in the ratio of forward to regurgitant blood flow.  Vasodilators with arterial effects (eg, nitroprusside) therefore help increase forward stroke volume and reduce pulmonary congestion in patients with MR and decompensated heart failure.

(Choices A, C and E)  A decrease in heart rate leads to an increase in venous return to the left ventricle (preload) due to increased diastolic filling time.  Increased LV preload causes an absolute increase in both forward and regurgitant blood flow (total stroke volume increases in accordance with the Frank-Starling mechanism).  Conversely, a reduction in venous return to the left ventricle decreases total stroke volume with absolute reductions in both forward and regurgitant flow.  However, the resulting change in the forward-to-regurgitant ratio is variable (mechanism/acuity dependent) and often modest; in contrast, reduced SVR will substantially increase the proportion of forward flow.

(Choice D)  An increase in LV contractility increases stroke volume and leads to an increase in both forward and regurgitant blood flow.  However, as the relative contribution of each pathway to LV afterload is unchanged, the ratio of forward to regurgitant blood flow remains the same.

Educational objective:In patients with mitral regurgitation, left ventricular afterload is determined by the balance of resistance between forward flow (aortic pressure) and regurgitant flow (left atrial pressure).  A reduction in systemic vascular resistance increases the ratio of forward to regurgitant blood flow and increases forward cardiac output.​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​
